title: Stacks, queues and linked lists
summary: Three simple structures defined by where things go in and come out, the interview classics built on them, and where they show up in AI apps.
youWillLearn: How a stack (last in, first out) powers undo and bracket matching
How a queue (first in, first out) keeps work in order, and why shift() can be slow
What a linked list is, and how to reverse one without losing it
How trimming a chat history for an LLM is a queue problem

glossary.stack: A list where you only add and remove at the top, so the last thing in is the first thing out (LIFO).
glossary.LIFO: Last in, first out: the newest item leaves first, like a pile of plates.
glossary.push: Add an item to the top of a stack or the end of a list.
glossary.pop: Remove and return the item on top of a stack.
glossary.queue: A list where you add at the back and remove from the front, so the first thing in is the first thing out (FIFO).
glossary.FIFO: First in, first out: the oldest item leaves first, like a line at a coffee shop.
glossary.linked list: A chain of items where each item holds its value plus a pointer to the next item, instead of sitting in numbered boxes.
glossary.pointer: A reference that says where another item is, so you can follow it there.
glossary.head: The first item of a linked list. If you lose it, you lose the whole list.
glossary.context window: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

steps.title: Undo: which change goes first?
body: Maya types a title in Notely, bolds a word, then deletes a line. She presses Cmd+Z.
Which change should come back? The last one: the deleted line. Press again, and the bold goes. The editor needs a structure where the newest item is always the easiest one to reach.

scene.caption: Three edits, newest on top. Undo needs the top one.

steps.title: Stacks: last in, first out
body: A stack only lets you touch the top. You push a new item onto the top, and you pop the top item off. Both are O(1).
That rule is called LIFO. In JavaScript, a plain array is a fine stack: push() and pop() both work at the end, so nothing shifts.

callout.text: A pile of plates. You put clean plates on top and take from the top. Nobody pulls a plate from the middle.

scene.caption: New edits are pushed on top. Undo pops the top.

steps.title: Stacks check brackets, too
body: A classic interview problem: is {[()]} balanced? Walk the string. Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, pop the top and check it is the matching opener.
If anything mismatches, or the stack is not empty at the end, it is unbalanced. One pass: O(n). Your program's call stack works the same way: the newest function call finishes first.

callout.text: Tools that parse streamed JSON from a model use the same idea: a stack of the braces and brackets still open tells them what has not closed yet.

scene.caption: Openers pile up. A closer must match whatever is on top.

steps.title: Queues: first in, first out
body: Now the opposite rule. Notely gets many AI summary jobs and should handle them in the order they arrived. That is a queue: add at the back, take from the front.
That rule is called FIFO. You met queues as services in system design. Inside an algorithm, the same shape keeps work in arrival order, and breadth-first search (next lesson) depends on it.

callout.text: A line at a coffee shop. New people join at the back. The barista serves whoever is at the front.

scene.caption: Jobs join at the back. The worker takes from the front.

steps.title: The shift() trap
body: In JavaScript, the obvious queue is an array with push() and shift(). But shift() removes index 0, and you saw in the last lesson what that costs: everything moves. O(n) per dequeue.
For a few dozen items, it does not matter. For a loop that dequeues thousands of times, keep a head index that moves forward instead of removing.

code.caption: A moving index instead of shift(). Fine for an algorithm that runs once.

scene.caption: shift() takes the front item, then every other item moves up one place.

steps.title: Linked lists: a chain of pointers
body: A linked list skips the numbered boxes. Each item holds its value and a pointer to the next item. You keep the first one, the head.

Adding at the head is O(1): point the new item at the old head. But reaching item 500 means following 500 pointers: O(n). You rarely build one in app code, but interviews love them for testing pointer care.

scene.caption: Each item points to the next. The last one points to nothing.

steps.title: Reverse a list without dropping it
body: The most asked linked list question: reverse it. Walk the chain once, flipping each next pointer to point backwards.
The trick is order. Save the next item before you overwrite the pointer, or you lose the rest of the chain. Three variables do it: prev, curr, next. O(n) time, O(1) space.

scene.caption: Every pointer now points backwards, and head moves to the old tail.

steps.title: Chat history is a queue
body: Notely adds "chat with your notes". Each request sends the conversation to Claude, but the model has a context window, and you also pay per token sent.
So you drop the oldest messages first until the rest fits a budget. First in, first out: a queue. Moving a start index forward, like the head trick, keeps it one pass.

code.caption: Real code trims whole turns, so a question never loses its answer. The system prompt is sent separately and never trimmed.

scene.caption: The oldest message leaves first so the newest ones fit the budget.

steps.title: Lost pointers and lost queues
body: Linked list bugs are nearly always pointer order: overwriting next before saving it, or reading .next on null. Draw boxes and arrows before coding; interviewers like seeing that.
In real apps, the bigger trap is an in-memory array used as a job queue. A serverless function can stop at any time, and the queued jobs vanish with it.

callout.text: If Claude Code keeps pending work in an array (jobs.push(…)) inside an API route, ask: "What happens to these jobs if the function restarts?" Real background work needs a durable queue or a jobs table. Also grep for shift() inside large loops.

scene.caption: Same row, now as jobs in an in-memory array. When the function stops, every job disappears.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A stack is last in, first out: undo, bracket matching, the call stack. A queue is first in, first out: jobs in order, chat history trimming, breadth-first search.
A linked list is a chain of pointers: O(1) to add at the head, O(n) to reach anything. Save next before you change it.

quiz.question: Notely wants a "back" button inside its note viewer that returns to the previously opened note, then the one before that. Which structure fits?

options.why: A queue would return the oldest note first, which is the opposite of how back should behave.
Back should return the most recently opened note first. Last in, first out. Browser history works the same way.
A map gives fast lookup by key, but it does not remember order the way back needs.

quiz.question: Claude Code wrote a breadth-first search that dequeues with queue.shift(), and it runs over 200,000 items. What should you ask for?

options.why: shift() removes index 0, so every remaining item moves. That is O(n) per call, and O(n²) over the whole search.

options.text: Switch to pop() so it is faster.
options.why: pop() is fast, but it takes the newest item. That turns the queue into a stack and changes the algorithm into depth-first search.

options.text: Keep a head index that moves forward instead of shifting.
options.why: Reading queue[head++] is O(1) and keeps first-in, first-out order.

quiz.question: While reversing a linked list, a candidate writes curr.next = prev as the first line inside the loop. What goes wrong?

options.text: The link to the rest of the list is overwritten before it was saved, so the loop cannot move forward.
options.why: After the flip, curr.next points backwards. Without saving the old next first, the rest of the chain is lost.

options.text: Nothing, the order of the lines does not matter.
options.why: Order is the whole trick. Pointers must be saved before they are overwritten.
The problem is not speed. The function loses the rest of the list and returns a wrong result.

takeaways: A stack is last in, first out: push() and pop() at the end of an array, both O(1).
A queue is first in, first out. shift() is O(n); a moving head index is O(1).
A linked list is O(1) to add at the head, O(n) to reach an item. Save next before you overwrite it.
Trimming a chat history to fit a model's context window is a queue: drop the oldest first.
Real background jobs need a durable queue or table, not an array in a serverless function.
